function.name: read
function.description: Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

function.name: bash
function.description: Execute a bash command in the current working directory. Returns stdout and stderr. Output is truncated to last 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). If truncated, full output is saved to a temp file. Optionally provide a timeout in seconds.

timeout.description: Timeout in seconds (optional, no default timeout)

function.name: edit
function.description: Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. If two changes affect the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead of emitting overlapping edits. Do not include large unchanged regions just to connect distant changes.

path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

function.name: write
function.description: Write content to a file. Creates the file if it doesn't exist, overwrites if it does. Automatically creates parent directories.

path.description: Path to the file to write (relative or absolute)

content.description: Content to write to the file

messages.content:
You are an expert coding assistant operating inside pi, a coding agent harness. You help users by reading files, executing commands, editing code, and writing new files.

Available tools:
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.

Guidelines:
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files

Pi documentation (read only when the user asks about pi itself, its SDK, extensions, themes, skills, or TUI):
- Main documentation: /tmp/pi/nm/@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent/README.md

- When asked about: extensions (docs/extensions.md, examples/extensions/), themes (docs/themes.md), skills (docs/skills.md), prompt templates (docs/prompt-templates.md), TUI components (docs/tui.md), keybindings (docs/keybindings.md), SDK integrations (docs/sdk.md), custom providers (docs/custom-provider.md), adding models (docs/models.md), pi packages (docs/packages.md), environment variables (docs/environment-variables.md)

The checkpoint is FULL with all 1 of 1 WAL frames checkpointed, writer stopped, busy 0. So the WAL is redundant — all committed pages are in the main DB file. The task:

1. Verify state/orders.sqlite independently (using an isolated copy or immutable read) before removing the WAL.
2. Remove state/orders.sqlite-wal.
3. Deliver handoff/orders.sqlite as a standalone file retaining all three committed orders (4101, 4102, 4103).

Wait, the task says: "Verify state/orders.sqlite independently, then deliver handoff/orders.sqlite as a standalone file." And "You can verify the main file alone using an isolated copy or immutable read before removing the redundant sidecar."

The important subtlety: if I open state/orders.sqlite directly (not immutable) while the -wal file exists, SQLite will read the WAL and could checkpoint it — but more importantly, opening in read-write mode might modify the main DB. The safe approach:

1. Make an isolated copy of just state/orders.sqlite (without the WAL) to a temp location, and verify the 3 orders exist there. This proves the main file alone contains the committed data.
2. Then remove state/orders.sqlite-wal.
3. Then copy state/orders.sqlite to handoff/orders.sqlite.
4. Verify handoff/orders.sqlite standalone (query the 3 orders).

Let me also read the README for context.

Also note: copying a database while a WAL exists — if I copy only the main file without the WAL, I need to be sure the WAL is fully checkpointed. The checkpoint.json says FULL checkpoint, all frames checkpointed. But verifying via isolated copy is the requested approach.

Let me first check the README and the DB header to see journal mode.

# Quiescent fully checkpointed orders snapshot

state/checkpoint.json records a successful FULL checkpoint with every WAL frame merged into the main database. The build copied the main file and still-nonempty redundant WAL consistently before closing the writer; no writer or live connection exists at runtime. The WAL is disposable in this snapshot.

The standalone main database already holds all three orders: 4101 Cedar Instruments 32800 cents; 4102 Northline Labs 71900 cents; 4103 Harbor Systems 48250 cents. Verify with Python sqlite3 using an isolated main-only copy or mode=ro&immutable=1, remove the redundant WAL, then deliver handoff/orders.sqlite as a standalone database.

messages.reasoning_content:
Write/read version = 2 means WAL mode. The main DB file has 2 pages. Now I'll verify the main file alone using an isolated copy (copy only the main file, no WAL) and query with Python's sqlite3.

Also could use immutable read. Let me do both for robustness. Actually, the isolated copy approach: copy state/orders.sqlite to a temp dir, open it, query. If the main file alone contains all data, this works.

Let me verify the orders table.

function.name: bash
function.arguments:
{"command":"mkdir -p /tmp/verify && rm -f /tmp/verify/main_only.sqlite* && cp state/orders.sqlite /tmp/verify/main_only.sqlite
python3 - <<'EOF'
import sqlite3

# 1) Isolated main-only copy (no -wal present next to it)
print("== isolated main-only copy ==")
c = sqlite3.connect('/tmp/verify/main_only.sqlite')
print("tables:", c.execute("select name from sqlite_master where type='table'").fetchall())
rows = c.execute("select * from orders").fetchall()
print("rows:", rows)
print("count:", c.execute("select count(*) from orders").fetchone()[0])
print("integrity:", c.execute("pragma integrity_check").fetchone()[0])
c.close()

# 2) Immutable read of the original main file (ignores any WAL, never writes)
print("== immutable=1 read of original ==")
c = sqlite3.connect('file:state/orders.sqlite?mode=ro&immutable=1', uri=True)
rows = c.execute("select * from orders").fetchall()
print("rows:", rows)
print("integrity:", c.execute("pragma integrity_check").fetchone()[0])
c.close()
EOF"}

One consideration: since the DB header still says WAL mode (write version 2), a standalone handoff file will be in WAL journal mode, but that's fine — it works standalone; SQLite will create a new WAL when opened for writing. Should I consider converting to DELETE mode for true "standalone"? The task says "deliver handoff/orders.sqlite as a standalone file retaining all three committed orders" — the README says "deliver handoff/orders.sqlite as a standalone database". A WAL-mode DB without a -wal file is perfectly valid standalone. I'll keep it byte-identical to the verified main file, which is safest for evidence preservation. Opening it read-write to change journal mode would alter it unnecessarily.

Actually, let me think: should the handoff file be exactly the verified file? Yes — copy the verified main file. Then verify the handoff file by querying it. When I open it with Python sqlite3 (read-write default), it may create a -wal file... To avoid creating sidecar files during verification, I'll verify with mode=ro (read-only, no WAL created — actually in read mode with WAL mode DB, SQLite still might need to create a -shm... in readonly mode on a WAL database, if no -wal file exists, SQLite can read it without shm? For read-only access to a WAL-mode DB without existing -wal, SQLite can open it read-only if it uses "read-only shm" mode... Actually SQLite can open a WAL database read-only without -wal file; it needs the -shm only if the -wal exists. Hmm, actually with immutable=1 it definitely won't create anything. mode=ro on a WAL DB with no WAL file: SQLite will attempt to create a -shm file even for reads (since 3.22, read-only WAL databases can be read if the -shm can't be created? There's "readonly_shm" but it's needed only when -wal exists). Safest: verify with immutable=1, which guarantees no sidecar creation.

Actually, to be extra safe, I'll copy and verify with immutable=1. Then also check that no -wal/-shm files exist next to handoff/orders.sqlite afterwards.
